lawyer:
Mr. S M Rezaul Karim, Advocate ------ for the Petitioner. 
Mr. A M. Aminuddin (A.A.G.) ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Alhaj Nazir Ahmed ------ Petitioner
Vs.
The National Board of Revenue and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the fixation of value in CRF No. HKK000040, HKK 000041, HKK 000042, HKK 000043 & HKK 000044 all dated 18.3.2000 at the rate of US$ 343.40 per Metric ton and assessment made on such value shall not be declared to have been held without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to assess customs duties and taxes on the basis of invoice value at the rate of US$ 223/- per Metric ton vide invoice Nos. BP 201314-A to BP 201314-E dated 28.2.2000 and/or such other order or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. In the writ petition it has been stated, inter alia, the petitioner opened a letter of credit No. SBL.KTG/CASH/023/2000 dated 15.2.2000 for importation of 500 Metric ton of Caustic Soda Solid through Standard Bank Limited Khatungoni Branch, Chittagong at the rate of US$ 2231- per metric ton as per the invoice No. BP 201314-A to BP 201314-E dated. 28.2.2000. Before the shipment of the aforesaid goods the petitioner arranged pre-shipment inspection in China as per SRO No. 40-Lw/2000/1817/Cus dated 8.2.2000 by respondent No. 3 who issued Clean Report of Findings Certificate in short CRF Certificate Nos. HKK000040, HKK 000041, HKK 000042, HKK 000043 & HKK 000044 all dated 18.3.2000. After arrival of the cargo in the Chittagong port the petitioner through his clearing agent submitted bill of entry registration Nos. C 273344, C 25351, C 27369 dated 23.4.2000 to the customs authority for assessment of customs duties taxes and other charges. The respondent No. 2 assessed the duties and charges on the basis of the impugned CRF value with endorsement values are for customs purposes only purported to have been fixed by the respondent No.3 as per the dictation of the customs authority, as such the said value is not a CRF value in the eye of law and the same cannot be the basis for assessment of duties and charges, hence the assessment endorsed on the bill of entry dated 23.4.2000 pursuant to the impugned CRF value is also impugned in the instant writ petition. Which has been alleged illegal and is of no legal effect. 

 3. The learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners submitted with reference to section 25A(2) of the Customs Act that in view of the provisions of law that the PSI Agency appointed under the PSI Order 1999 for verifying and certifying in the prescribed manner the price, quantity, quality and customs classification for the imports in question which shall be accepted as the basis for the assessment of customs duties, VAT and other charges and in view of the provisions of Article 5(Ka)of the Pre-shipment Inspection Order, 1999 that the PSI Agency shall endorse the price, description, quality, quantity and customs classification in the invoice and packing list and upon ascertaining its worth shall issue the certificate in accordance with law and then shall certify the CRF certificate in the prescribed manner under the provisions of Article 7(Kha) (q) of the said order maintaining the certified price as per GATT valuation agreement, the PSI agency has acted contrary to the provisions of law and Order in not verifying and certifying the price of the import on ascertaining the correctness worth of the value of the import to be the CIF value in the certificate itself inasmuch as the PSI Agency having endorsed the price of the import on the invoice and packing list as acceptable, acted contrary thereto in putting highly inflated and fictitious value as the CIF value in the certificate rendering the certificate not in accordance with law and void. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the respondent PSI Agency has failed to perform the statutory obligation ascertaining differently the CIF price of the import as contemplated under Article 7 while accepting the price appearing in the invoice and packing list and acted contrary to the provision of Jaw and the PSI Order putting inflated CIF value to be the certified price of the import inasmuch as the PSI Agency thereby surreptitiously put-ting an imaginary CRF value thereby cheating the importer which amounts to misconduct on the part of the CRF Agency. The learned Advocate has further submitted with reference to Annexure-C(1) that the petitioner having pointed out the discrepancy to the PSI Agency and not having been replied and there being violation of the law and PSI Order, 1999 and CRF Certificate not being in accordance with law and this application was maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution inasmuch as no fact need be decided but the decision could be had on the basis of interpretation of the provision of Customs Act and PSI Order, 1999 by way of judicial review by this Court. 

 4. The learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the respondents I and 4 taking us through the annexures and the affidavit-in-opposition has submitted that the obligation of the PSI Agency to get the price verified and certified in the prescribed manner shall be accepted as the basis for assessment but any discrepancy as to the price found in the endorsement of the invoice and in the packing list with the CIF value would not render the certificate illegal as the said CIF value was the result of ascertaining the correctness thereof, which may differ with the invoice value certified and endorsed by the PSI Agency either in invoice or packing list. The learned Deputy Attorney General with Mr. A.M. Aminuddin and Mr. M. Khaled Ahmed have however, extraneously argued that the said ascertainment of CIF value which is different from the C & F value being the basis for assessment by the customs authority, the customs authority are obliged to accept the certifying CIF value for the purpose of assessment of customs duty, vat and other charges. The learned Deputy Attorney General has further submitted that if the petitioner disagreed with the certified CIF value the importer could take recourse to Article 9 of PSI Order raising dispute firstly with the PSI Agency then with review committee then finally in an appeal both under the provisions of section 193C of the Customs Act and under the provision of Article 9 of PSI Order and in view of the specific efficacious remedy pro-vided thereunder, according to the learned Deputy Attorney General, this applications under Article 102 of the Constitution are not maintainable. Section 25A as amended on 30th June 1999 runs as under: 

 (6) For the purposes of this section `price' means value of the goods determined in accordance with sub section (1) and (2) of Section 25. 

 5. Thus, it appears that the government shall appoint pre-shipment inspection agencies and prescribe and determine the manner and the scope of their certification and related matters and that the government as well on that basis make assessment of customs duties, VAT and other charges relying on the certificate issued in the prescribed manner by the PSI agencies as to the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any imported goods duly verified and certified by the said agency and the price that has been verified and certified would be the value of the goods i.e. normal value as determined under sub-section (1) and (2) of section 25. In order to carry out the purpose of the said section to provide the prescribed manner, the government has issued Pre-shipment Order, 1999 vide SRO No. 316-Law/99/1807/Cus dated 19.10.99 published in the Bangladesh Gazette, Additional Issue (Extraordinary) providing for the provision for the appointment of PSI agency and determine the scope and manner of their certification and related matters. Article 5(1)(Ka) thereof provides duties and the function on the PSI agency inter alia, as under:- 

 7. Thus, it appears that the procedure laid down in Article 7 is that the certified price must be as per GATT valuation agreement .0 in prescribed form appendix (7) and that the letter of credit shall mention the name of PSI agency and the L/C shall contain a condition that the invoice and the packing list shall be endorsed and that the number and date of CRF certificate would be mentioned in the invoice and the packing list and the copy of the letter of credit has to be sent to the local office PSI agency by the concerned Bank. Thus, from the above, inters duty is cast upon the importer to mention name of the PSI agency in the letter of credit and the PSI agency shall also in its turn while endorsing invoice and packing list issued by the exporter shall also mention the number of certificate with date on those papers and that the PSI agency shall mention the CIF price in the CRF certificate. Article 7 provides that if it appears to PSI agency at the time of inspection that the declaration of the exporter on any subject other than the price is not justifiable and the exporter finds it difficult to meet the discrepancy or refuses to do so, then PSI agency shall issue Non-Negotiable Report of Finding (NNRF) in form in Appendix 8. 

 8. Article 8 of PSI order 1999 provides that if the quantity, quality, description customs classification and the price of the import has been certified and if the invoice, packing list and certificate is in accordance with law and Order, the same would be the basis for assessment. Thus, the PSI agency shall after ascertaining the correctness of the price etc, shall endorse the same in the packing list and invoice supplied by the exporter and then certify as to the CIF of the import in the CRF certificate which shall be according to the GATT valuation agreement. Clause 3 of Article 2 of the General Agreement of Tariffs and Trade (GATI) provides as under; 

 "3. If in applying this Article, more than one transaction value of identical goods is found, the lowest such value shall be used to determine the customs value of the imported goods." 

 10. On perusal of invoice of packing list it appears that PSI agency has, upon verification of the price, put an endorsement on the packing list and invoice and has accepted the same and having accepted the same the certificate must reflect the said acceptance, instead an inflated CIF price has been mentioned in CRF Certificate. 

 11. The PSI agency has duly verified and endorsed the invoice price as accepted value and certified to that effect on the body of the invoice and the packing list. 

 12. Now coming to the aforesaid provision of law the PSI agency though has a legal obligation to verify the correctness of the invoice value and to issue the certificate putting CIF price of the import in consonance thereof but in the instant cases the C&F price having been accepted on verification and endorsed accordingly in the invoice and packing list, PSI agency could not put in an imaginary amount as CIF value, which is very much inflamed and fictitious one. 

 13. As we already stated that there are provision for correction of the clerical error under Article 5(উ) after ascertainment of the correctness in Article 5(Ka) but the same has to be done within three days of the issuance of certificate. Admittedly, the respondent No. 3 did not provide the break up of the clarification for putting CIF value. The respondent has, however, tried to justify the CIF price by putting the CRF certificate denying any collusion as alleged between the customs authority and the CRF agency. Whether there may be collusion or not but the said respondents also could not justify that the procedure of law and order have been followed in ascertaining the correctness of the CIF value put in the CRF certificate, once having endorsed the C&F value as accepted. 

 14. The facts and circumstances of the case go to show that the endorsement 'value for customs purpose may differ' is not contemplated under the provisions of law and Order and such arbitrary, fictitious CIF value put in CRF certificate cannot be the basis for assessment and any assessment thereon is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority. The CRF certificate with such endorsement namely, value for customs purpose may differ cannot be relied to make the certificate in accordance with law and the same would not be the price as mentioned in sub-section (3) of section 25A. Sub-section (1) and (2) of section 25 of the Customs Act authorize the department to assess normal price of the goods/import in question in the Rule considering the contemporary commercial price of the goods at the place of origin with notice to the importer or agent to produce any document or paper in support of their invoice value which shall be the basis for ascertainment of the normal price in the event of cancellation of the CRF certificate. 

 15. Now coming to the case of the respondents we like to observe that the department has also a duty to see as to whether the PSI agency has performed their obligation in accordance with law and see the justification of the CIF value put in duly verified by the PSI agency upon ascertaining the correctness or worth of the C&F price appearing in the invoice and packing list. Such obligation has to discharged ascertaining the C&F value in the invoice and packing list and endorsing the same there of under Article 5(Ka) and 7(cha) and then put the C&F value in the CRF certificate. The department as well has a duty see that the value endorsed to be correct in the invoice and packing list by the PSI agency should tally with the CIF value in the CRF Certificate to be the basis of assessment. In case of disagreement by endorsement like value for customs purposes only differ would surely render the CRF certificate unacceptable to be the basis of assessment. 

 "It is only when a provision of appeal in .a statute is attended with an inviolable and non-relaxable condition of payment of fine or extra duty in full that it can be said that the petitioner has no equally efficacious remedy." 

 17. In the case of 51 DLR 206 it has been held that "mere allegation of violation of the provisions of law cannot give rise to any cause of action for filing a writ petition when there is forum for seeking remedy against the impugned orders. Since the petitioner did not avail of the alternative forum of appeal as provided in the Customs Act and the said forum being an equally efficacious one for his remedy the rule obtained in this case should be discharged and referred the case of Delecia Diary Food Ltd. Vs. Collector of Customs 51 DLR (HC) 382 if the learned Assistant Attorney General further submitted that the petitioner is aggrieved by any order of assessment made by Collector of Customs or by Customs officer under the Collector of Customs, he is to file review and then an appeal provided under the Custom Act. In view of the above, the learned Deputy Attorney General has further submitted that the instant cases without exhausting those remedies, the petitioners cannot invoke the writ jurisdiction and referred the case of Trade Channel Vs. Collector of Customs reported in 44 DLR 127. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that where there are questions of law and interpretation of the statutory provisions remedy by way of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution is maintainable and in this respect he referred the decision in the case of M/s. Usmania. Glass Sheet Factory Ltd. Vs. Sales Tax Officer, Companies Circle reported in 22 DLR (SC) 437 wherein it has been held: 

 "Before coming to the merits of the case it will be convenient to dispose of here the preliminary objections raised on behalf of the respondent that the writ petition was liable to be dismissed as the cause of action against the respondent was premature and the Appellant should have pursued the legal remedies provided in the Sales Tax Act- for appeal and revision to the higher authorities. Mr. Abdul Matin Khan Chowdhury learned counsel for the respondent contended that the writ petition filed by the appellant was not maintainable because it was premature. According to the learned counsel no assessment has been made for the sales tax and unless it is made, the appellant has no cause of action to challenge it in the High Court. The contention of the learned counsel has not impressed it is not disputed that the appellant had to filed return of the sale of goods and under section 12(1) of the sales of the sale of goods. In the recent case, the appellant filed 14 revised Returns on the 20th of March 1965 and claimed therein that glass sheet was exempted from the payment of sales tax. On the 31st March, 1965 the Sales Tax Officer called upon the appellant to submit its explanation by the 18th April, 1965 failing which action was to be taken to realize the arrears of sales tax on the basis of Returns filed previously. The appellant submitted its explanation on the 1st April, 1965. The Central Government also agreed with the Central Board of Revenue. Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant on the 22nd, June, 1965 and called upon it to pay all the arrears of salestak within June, 1965. In my opinion, on the facts of the present case, the appellant was entitled to protect itself from the threat of the department to realize the arrears of sales tax. It is not disputed that the sales tax for the period from March 1961 to 20th of March 1965 was about RS. 4,00,000/- out of it's the appellant has failed to pay about Rs. 2,00,000/- it cannot, therefore, be said that the writ petition was pre-mature or the appellant had no cause of action against the respondent to ventilate its grievance against him. The objection of the respondent that the appellant had alternative remedies by departmental means is also not of much substance. It has been held by this Court that in a case where the dispute arises between the parties in respect of a fiscal right based upon a statutory instrument the same can be easily determined in writ jurisdiction. 

 "To the same effect there is a decision of this Court in the case of Pakistan and another Vs.Qazi Ziauddin (2). This point was also considered in the case of Abdul Ghani and another Vs. Government of Pakistan and others (3). It was held in that case "anything done beyond or in excess of powers conferred by statute can be brought within the power of avoidance vested in the High Court. In such a case, the High Court can examine if the Officer concerned has acted in accordance with the powers conferred upon him by the statute." I would, therefore, repel the preliminary objections raised on behalf of the respondent." 

 In the case of Abdul Ghani and another Vs. Subedar Shoedar Khan Company and others reported in PLD 1968 (SC)131 it has been held: 

 "Anything done beyond or in excess of power conferred by statute can be brought within the power of avoidance vested in the High Court. In such a case the High Court can examine if the officer concerned has acted in accordance with the powers conferred upon him by the statute. If he acts within his power, section 60 will operate as a bar to the jurisdiction of the Court, but when he acts in exercise of his power, his order is susceptible in interference by the High Court in his submit jurisdiction. 

 " It is profitable to refer to the case of Mahboob Ali Mallik Vs. Province of West Pakistan, 15 DLR (West Pak.) 129 wherein it has been held: 

 "If there is no other authority which has the power to give relief of the requisite nature and extent, it is the duty of this Court in a fit case to give that relief if it has the power to do so under Article 98. There is nothing in Article 98 which would release this Court, in such a case, from that obligation, merely because it would be necessary to take evidence, whether oral or documentary, before relief could be given." 

 In the result, this Rule is made absolute in the terms mentions in the body of the judgment directing the department to determine normal value of the goods imported by the respective petitioner in accordance with law ignoring the arbitrary and fictitious CIF value certified by the CRF agency.
